title: Modal Meadow
intro: Must, have to, should, might. Pick the modal that says what the sentence means: obligation, advice or possibility.

A2.q: You ___ wear a seatbelt in the car. It's the law.
A2.why: “It's the law” means a rule with no choice: must.

A2.q: There's no choice: my boss says I ___ finish this report by Friday.
A2.why: “No choice” means obligation from outside, here the boss: have to.

A2.q: You ___ study more if you want to pass.
A2.why: Friendly advice (“if you want to pass”): should.

A2.q: It ___ rain later — take an umbrella just in case.
A2.why: “Just in case” shows we are not sure: might for possibility.

A2.q: Students ___ arrive on time for class.
A2.why: A school rule for everyone: must.

A2.q: You ___ see a doctor about that cough.
A2.why: Giving advice to a friend: should.

A2.q: We ___ leave now or we'll miss the train.
A2.why: “Or we'll miss the train” leaves no choice: have to.

A2.q: She ___ be at home — I'm not sure.
A2.why: “I'm not sure” means only a possibility: might.

A2.q: You ___ eat vegetables — they're good for you.
A2.why: “They're good for you” is advice: should.

A2.q: Passengers ___ show their passports at the gate. No passport, no flight.
A2.why: “No passport, no flight” is a strict rule: must.

A2.q: Welcome to Dodge City: you ___ hand in your gun to the sheriff. It's the rule.
A2.why: “It's the rule” means no choice: must.

A2.q: It ___ be windy at the Malvarrosa this afternoon — maybe take a jacket.
A2.why: “Maybe” shows we are not sure: might.

B1.q: You ___ smoke in here — it's forbidden.
B1.why: “Forbidden” means it is not allowed: mustn't.

B1.q: You ___ come if you don't want to — it's optional.
B1.why: “Optional” means no obligation: don't have to. Mustn't would forbid it.

B1.q: It ___ be him — his car isn't outside.
B1.why: We are sure it is impossible (no car): can't. Mustn't is for rules, not deductions.

B1.q: We ___ book in advance, but it's a good idea.
B1.why: “But it's a good idea” means it is not necessary, only helpful: don't have to.
A strong guess that it is true: must. “You must be joking!” is a fixed phrase.

B1.q: The coach is running late. It ___ arrive by 9, but I'm not certain.
B1.why: “I'm not certain” means only a possibility: could.

B1.q: You were rude to her yesterday. You really ___ apologise.
B1.why: After being rude, the right thing to do is to say sorry: should for advice.
A museum rule against doing something: mustn't.

B1.q: She ___ be at home — all the lights are on.
B1.why: The lights are strong evidence, so you are sure: must be.

B1.q: You ___ need a visa — check the requirements.
B1.why: “Check the requirements” shows we don't know yet: might for possibility.

B1.q: Dr Snow says the water from this pump is dirty. You ___ drink it!
B1.why: A strong warning not to do something: mustn't.

B1.q: The Lonja in Valencia is free on Sundays, so you ___ pay to go in.
B1.why: “Free” means paying is not necessary: don't have to.

B2.q: You ___ have worried — everything was fine.
B2.why: You worried, but it wasn't necessary: needn't have + past participle.

B2.q: The meeting ___ start at 10, but it's often late.
B2.why: What the plan says, not what really happens (“often late”): is supposed to.

B2.q: You ___ to apologise for that — it was rude.
B2.why: Ought is the only one that takes “to”. Should and must never do.

B2.q: After an announcement like that, prices are ___ to rise — it always happens.
B2.why: “It always happens” means it is almost certain: bound to.

B2.q: You ___ have told me — I would have helped.
B2.why: Criticism of something that didn't happen in the past: should have + past participle.

B2.q: He ___ know the answer — he studied this yesterday.
B2.why: He studied, so we expect him to know: ought to for a reasonable expectation.

B2.q: You ___ have finished it so soon — there was no rush.
B2.why: “No rush” means it wasn't necessary, but you did it: needn't have.

B2.q: It's getting late — we ___ to leave soon.
B2.why: Only ought takes “to”: ought to = should.

B2.q: The train ___ to arrive at six, according to the timetable.
B2.why: “According to the timetable” is the plan: is supposed to.

B2.q: Given the forecast, it's ___ to rain this weekend.
B2.why: The forecast makes it almost certain: bound to.

B2.q: Doctors ___ have washed their hands before surgery, but in the 1840s almost nobody did.
B2.why: The right thing that didn't happen in the past: should have + past participle.

B2.q: The stagecoach ___ to leave at noon, but the driver is still in the saloon.
B2.why: The plan says noon, but reality is different: is supposed to.

C1.q: She ___ have missed the train — she wasn't on it when it got in.
C1.why: She wasn't on the train, so we are almost sure: must have + past participle.

C1.q: He ___ have seen the email — he replied within minutes.
C1.why: His quick reply proves it: must have for a confident deduction.

C1.q: You ___ have told him — now he's upset.
C1.why: Regret about a past action that caused trouble: shouldn't have.

C1.q: They ___ have left already — their car's still here.
C1.why: The car proves it is impossible: can't have + past participle.

C1.q: I ___ have bought so much food — half of it went to waste.
C1.why: I bought it, but it wasn't necessary: needn't have.

C1.q: It ___ have been a difficult decision for her — she lay awake for weeks.
C1.why: Weeks without sleep make us almost sure: must have.

C1.q: You ___ have gone to all that trouble, but thank you.
C1.why: “Needn't have gone” means you did it although it wasn't necessary; “didn't need to” is followed by a bare verb, not “have gone”.

C1.q: It was his own fault: he ___ have checked the risks before investing.
C1.why: “His own fault” is criticism: should have. Ought would need “to”.

C1.q: She ___ have forgotten — she never forgets birthdays.
C1.why: “She never forgets” makes it impossible: can't have.

C1.q: We ___ have left earlier — the traffic was terrible.
C1.why: Regret about the past: should have, because we left too late.

C1.q: The outlaws ___ have crossed the river — their tracks stop at the water's edge.
C1.why: The tracks are the clue that makes us almost sure: must have.

C1.q: The Romans ___ have eaten Valencian rice — it only arrived with the Moors.
C1.why: Rice came after the Romans, so it is impossible: can't have.
